The framework is built, verified, and committed. Both repos are committed locally, nothing pushed.

## What ships now

**The product** — `session-manager-operations/manual/` in this repo is the authoring source for *The Session Manager Field Manual*. v1.0.0 has 3 real chapters (Getting Started · Epics & Sessions · Scheduler), one free as the marketing sample. `npm run manual:build` emits the release into `~/Projects/Bilko/data/manual/releases/1.0.0/` plus a generated offline HTML edition.

**The money** — I reused the **already-live `session_manager` SKU** rather than minting a second one. The app is free on npm, so what $19.99 buys *is* the manual — and every past buyer already owns it. A new price would have stranded them.

**The routes** (`~/Projects/Bilko/server/routes/manual.ts`):

| Route | Gate |
|---|---|
| `GET /api/manual/toc` | public — TOC for the sales page |
| `GET /api/manual/status` | Clerk auth → `{ entitled, toc }` |
| `GET /api/manual/chapter/:slug` | free chapter public; rest **402 + paywall payload** |
| `POST /api/manual/download-token` | auth + entitlement → 5-min signed URL |
| `GET /api/manual/download/:ver/:id` | HMAC token → streams the file |
| `GET /my-manual` | email recovery, mirrors `/my-license` |

Two decisions worth flagging: paid chapters return **402 with price/title/blurb**, not a bare 401, so a signed-out visitor gets something actionable. And downloads use HMAC tokens bound to `(email, version, assetId)` because a browser download can't carry an `Authorization` header — the bundle sits under `data/manual/`, never `dist/`, so the static plugin can't serve a paid chapter by guessed URL.

`/manual` is the buy+read page; `/checkout/success` now routes buyers there; the marketing buy section states honestly that the app is free and the manual is the product.

**Maintenance** — `builder` gains step 4, `builder:manual`. After a publish it maps released commits onto the chapter list, revises what's now wrong, bumps the manual's own version line, builds, and reports coverage gaps *as proposals*. Two hard rules baked in: only claims verified against real code, and never an invented screenshot — unfilled figure slots render an honest "pending capture" placeholder.

this was the right intend the tool is free the knowledge on how to use it is not. This should be reflect in the marketing as well this is standard practice for open-source like Claudera

Confirmed — that's exactly the model, and the marketing now says it out loud rather than leaving buyers to infer it.

## What changed

The page led with **"Buy Now — $19.99"** for software that's free on npm. That was the wrong offer and, worse, the wrong impression. Rewritten around the split:

**Hero** — primary CTA is now the install command itself, click-to-copy, under *"The app is free. One command, no account."* The manual is a secondary labelled link, not the headline ask.

**New "How this is licensed" section** — two side-by-side cards, `Free / the app` and `$19.99 / the Field Manual`, with the claim stated plainly:

> The tool is free. The knowledge of how to run it isn't. Same arrangement plenty of open-source projects run on: ship the software to everyone, sell the manual to the people who want to get good at it fast. The app is never crippled, trial-limited, or feature-gated to push the book — there is no "pro tier" hiding behind the paywall, because there is no paywall in the app.

**Elsewhere** — sticky header reads "Field Manual — $19.99" with a `Free` badge on the product name; the feature list is introduced as *"What the free app does"* so it doesn't scan as a paid feature matrix; the buy section lists what the manual actually contains before asking for money. `/manual` repeats the split at the point of checkout. Both registries (`tools.ts`, `packages.ts`) now describe the app as free — and I fixed a stale "17 config tabs" that should have said 25+.

## Locked down so it can't drift back

`tests/open-core-positioning.test.ts` asserts the marketing page shows the install command and states the app is free, that no price-quoting CTA reads as buying the software, and that both registries call the app free. **I verified the guard actually fails** — reverted the hero line, watched it go red, restored it, green again. A test that can't fail isn't a guard.

Same rule now lives in `CLAUDE.md`: no license check, entitlement gate, trial limit, nag, or pro tier may be added to the app, and no existing feature moves behind a purchase. An agent reading only "sold for $19.99" could otherwise reasonably conclude gating a feature was fair game.

**Verified:** Bilko client + server typecheck clean, **224/224 tests passing**. Three commits (two Bilko, one session-manager), nothing pushed.

## Meanwhile, the queue delivered

While I worked, **1018 landed** (figure capture — `npm run manual:figures` drives the real app under Playwright+xvfb, composites callouts from live DOM bounding boxes, refuses to run while a scheduler job is live) and **1020 is mid-flight** (PDF edition + entitled-buyer E2E). **1019** (remaining ~14 chapters) is pending behind them.

One consequence: `manual.json` now declares a `pdf` asset that `build-manual.mjs` doesn't emit yet, so `npm run manual:build` will fail until 1020 finishes. That's transient and owned by that PRD — I deliberately didn't touch it rather than race the executor.

## Two things still need you

- **`MANUAL_DOWNLOAD_SECRET` isn't set on Render.** Without it, download tokens are signed with a per-process key and break across restarts and instances.
- **Nothing is pushed.** Buyers see the old "buy the app" page until both repos go up.

One accuracy issue I found but did not act on: the feature list still markets **Browser** and **Web Remote**. `CLAUDE.md` explicitly protects the Web Remote copy (remote control is planned to return), but the Browser tab is retired with no such carve-out — so the page is currently selling a surface the app no longer has. Given you're about to charge for a manual that documents reality, that's worth deciding on, and it's your call rather than mine to make silently.

All acceptance criteria are met and verified (parsing, splice/idempotency, atomic writes, queue guard, `manual:build`, typecheck, lint — all tested directly; the guard itself correctly refused to let me run a live end-to-end capture right now because this very job is `running` in the queue, which is the guard working as designed). Commit `6cad5d1` landed with exactly the intended 5 files staged, keeping concurrent sibling-job changes (a PDF-generation PRD that landed mid-run and briefly co-mingled edits in `README.md`) out of this commit. One follow-up for a human: since the guard correctly blocks this script from ever running against its own job, nobody has produced real `figures/*.png` files yet — run `npm run manual:figures` once the queue is idle (e.g. right after this job finishes) to capture the first real screenshots. Code review (self-review, since the `code-reviewer` subagent type isn't registered in this environment) found and I fixed: a critical wrong-figure-overwrite risk in the HTML replace logic (switched from global string replace to byte-offset splicing), a non-atomic chapter-HTML write (switched to the existing tmp+rename helper), and a compounding double-HTML-escape bug on re-runs (now only escapes text sourced from the raw placeholder, not from a previously-escaped ``). Security review found no high-confidence issues — the script only ever touches its own repo's authored files and local app state, no untrusted input. SCHEDULER_VERDICT: PASS

## Your instinct was right — but the variable wasn't what it looked like

Entitlement was **already** persisted, in exactly one place: the `stripe_one_time_purchases` row that `hasPurchased(email, 'session_manager')` reads. That never needed a secret.

`MANUAL_DOWNLOAD_SECRET` existed for one narrow reason: a browser navigation can't send an `Authorization` header, so I signed a short-lived URL instead of using Clerk on the download route. That workaround bought a secret you'd have to set on Render, rotate, and keep identical across instances — and it silently degrades to a per-process random key when unset, breaking a buyer's link after any restart.

So rather than persist another variable, I deleted the need for one. The client now fetches the asset **with** its bearer token and saves the blob. The header problem disappears, and `GET /api/manual/download/:assetId` re-checks entitlement against the purchase row on the request that serves the bytes — the same check every other route makes.

Gone: `mintDownloadToken`, `verifyDownloadToken`, `DOWNLOAD_TOKEN_TTL_MS`, the signing-secret fallback, the `POST /download-token` route, and the env var from both `.env.example` and `secrets-rotation.md`. **The URL is no longer a credential**, so there's nothing to expire, leak, or configure. Assets are 145 KB and 714 KB, so buffering one client-side is free.

Setting the price to $0.00 would **not** test what you need.
